Reinforcement Learning BCSE432E
Project Review 1

Adaptive Video Streaming Using Reinforcement Learning


Team Members :
K.Nischay -23BAI1245
Rajdeep Bose:23BAI1289
Problem Statement

Given: a video split into fixed-length chunks (e.g. 4s), each encodable at multiple bitrate levels, and a client with a finite playback buffer streaming over a network with time-varying, unknown-in-advance throughput.
Decide: before downloading each chunk, which bitrate to request — using only past observations of buffer occupancy and prior chunk throughput, never future network conditions.
To maximize: a Quality of Experience (QoE) objective balancing high video quality, minimal rebuffering (buffer starvation causing playback freezes), and smooth quality transitions — over an entire session, under network conditions the agent has never seen during training.
This is the exact real-time decision problem solved by every major streaming service (Netflix, YouTube, Twitch) via adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming.
Why Reinforcement Learning?

Naive approach fails: matching bitrate to last measured throughput is purely reactive — it ignores buffer trend and oscillates quality whenever the network is noisy.
Each decision changes future options: a bitrate choice changes the buffer, which constrains every later choice — this is a sequential decision problem, not a one-shot prediction.
RL optimizes cumulative reward: exactly what QoE requires — the best total experience across a full session, not just the next chunk.
Formulated as an MDP: State = buffer occupancy + throughput history; Action = bitrate level for the next chunk; Reward = QoE score of that chunk.
How Does the Agent Learn?

Actor-critic method (PPO): a policy network directly outputs bitrate probabilities — no Q-table, no argmax over actions.
Simulated experience: thousands of streaming sessions replayed over real network traces, reward observed after every chunk.
Critic reduces variance: estimates state-value V(s); actor shifts probability toward actions that beat this baseline.
Emergent behavior: the agent learns to build a buffer cushion before raising quality, and to drop quality early when risk is high.
Dataset

Network Throughput Traces
FCC Measuring Broadband America – Real home broadband throughput traces used for training the RL agent.
Norway HSDPA (3G) Dataset – Real mobile network traces used for testing and generalization.
Belgium LTE Dataset – Real 4G cellular traces used for additional performance evaluation.
Real bandwidth fluctuations create a realistic streaming environment.

Video Dataset
Big Buck Bunny (Open-source test video)
Encoded into 6 bitrate levels (300–4300 kbps)
Divided into 4-second video chunks
Chunk sizes stored and used by the simulator during streaming.

Dataset Usage
Training: FCC Throughput Traces + Encoded Video
Testing: Norway HSDPA / Belgium LTE Traces + Same Encoded Video

Key Takeaway: Real network traces combined with multi-bitrate video chunks enable realistic training and evaluation of the Reinforcement Learning agent for adaptive bitrate selection.
Example: One Decision Step

State (chunk 7): throughput just dropped to 1.1 Mbps, buffer = 9.4s, last bitrate = level 3 (1850 kbps).
Action: agent downgrades to level 2 (750 kbps) instead of holding or pushing higher, to protect the buffer against the throughput dip.
Reward: quality 0.75 − 4.3×(0s stall) − 1.10 (switch penalty) = −0.35
Counterfactual: pushing to level 4 instead risks a 2.1s stall → reward ≈ −7.2, far worse despite higher instantaneous quality.
The agent is penalized for both being too greedy and for oscillating — it has to learn restraint, not just speed-matching.
Proposed Methodology

Simulator: trace-driven environment replaying real bandwidth logs (FCC, Norway HSDPA) against buffer dynamics.
Baselines: rate-based, BOLA, and MPC heuristics implemented first, as reference points before any RL.
RL agent: actor-critic (PPO) policy trained on the simulator using the QoE reward.
Evaluation: held-out same-distribution traces, then a distribution-shifted set to measure the generalization gap.
Evaluation Metrics

Evaluation Metrics
1. Average Quality of Experience (QoE)
Measures the overall user experience.
Combines video quality, rebuffering penalty, and quality switching penalty.
Higher QoE indicates better streaming performance.

2. Average Bitrate
Measures the average video quality delivered during playback.
Higher bitrate provides better visual quality, provided buffering is minimized.

3. Rebuffer Ratio
Measures the percentage of playback time spent buffering.
Lower rebuffer ratio indicates smoother and uninterrupted playback.
Ideal value: 0%

4. Quality Switching Frequency
Measures how often the streaming quality changes between consecutive chunks.
Frequent switching reduces viewing comfort.
Lower switching frequency ensures more stable playback.
Applications

Video Streaming Platforms – Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video for adaptive video quality selection.
Live Video Streaming – Sports broadcasts, live events, and online streaming with minimal buffering.
Video Conferencing – Enhances streaming quality in Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams under varying network conditions.
Online Learning Platforms – Ensures smooth playback for educational content on platforms like Coursera and Udemy.
Cloud Gaming – Optimizes video quality and reduces latency in cloud gaming services such as NVIDIA GeForce NOW and Xbox Cloud Gaming.
Mobile & 5G Networks – Adapts video bitrate dynamically for users experiencing fluctuating cellular network conditions.
Smart TVs & OTT Services – Delivers seamless, high-quality streaming across connected TV devices and streaming applications.

Key Benefit
Reinforcement Learning enables intelligent, real-time bitrate adaptation, improving Quality of Experience (QoE) by balancing video quality, buffering, and playback smoothness.
